generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, an effective search is a process, not a single lookup. You plan what you are after, choose keywords that capture it, search a tool such as your library discovery service or a database, weigh which results are suitable, and follow references to reach further work. At this stage the point is to see the whole shape of a good search; weighing sources and extending a search are skills that later courses build in full.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students are asked to find sources on the same topic for a seminar.

{{learner-a}} opens the library search tool, types the topic in, and uses the first result on the list. The job feels done. But {{learner-a}} skipped almost every stage: no plan, no thought about keywords, no weighing of the source, and no second look. It was one lookup, and whatever came first. This is a one-off lookup, not an effective search.

{{learner-b}} first sets an objective and picks keywords, then searches the tool, glances over the results to judge which look suitable, and follows a reference from the best one to a further source. Her search moved through the stages in order. This is an effective, planned search.

Both students searched the same tool. Only {{learner-b}} worked through the stages that make a search effective.
generatedProse.summary: An effective search is a planned process with stages: plan, identify keywords, use a search tool, evaluate what you find, and extend the search. You can now describe these stages and recognise effective searching as a process rather than a one-off lookup. The next lesson takes the first two stages, planning and keywords, and shows you how to do them yourself.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s search effective rather than a one-off lookup?

items.text: She worked through the stages: planned, chose keywords, searched, weighed and extended.
She used the library tool instead of a search engine.
She used the very first result the search returned.
She finished the task in a single step.

feedback.correct: That's right. Moving through the stages in order is what makes a search effective.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} DID across the search, not which tool she opened.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}}'s search was effective because she worked through the stages. Using the tool, taking the first result, or finishing in one step are not what made the difference.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
